about: Wardley maps of ruv.sgit as a business: one for the whole and one per offer. Evolution (x) runs genesis 0 to commodity 1 (stage edges at 0.17, 0.4, 0.7); visibility (y) runs 1 at the user to 0 out of sight. Positions are judgements, not measurements: a map, not a measurement. Group colours and shapes come from the site's theme tokens (assets/maps.js). Drawn for run r5-market, 15 Oct 2026.

whole.title: ruv.sgit as a business
whole.user: A consultant, company or internal team
whole.need: agent work done under a policy, with a record they keep

components.label: AgentDB / RuVector
components.note: Agent memory and vector search. MIT, by rUv / ruvnet.

components.label: Coding agents (Claude Code)
components.note: The workers in every run so far are Claude Code subagents.

components.label: Model tokens
components.note: Bought by the million; our key or the customer's.

components.label: AWS compute and storage

whole.reading: The user sees one thing, governed agent work, and it is still custom: every run so far is assembled by hand. Everything heavy under it is bought or borrowed: rUv's Ruflo hive and AgentDB/RuVector are products we build on, the model tokens and AWS are commodities, and sgit vaults are our own product. The move is to productise the middle, so that a task run, an ABP and a delivered vault become things with a price and a size, and to let vault storage drift toward commodity. What stays custom is the expert's judgement and the policy written for one customer; that is where the margin is, because nobody can buy it by the token. Not claimed: runs are not automated end to end yet, and dedicated compute is designed, not built (SG Compute is not connected to runs).

runs.reading: This is the offer we are commoditising hardest. The user sees a run with a price; under it, the hive is rUv's product, the workers and the tokens are bought, and the vault is ours. The run itself is custom today because a person drives each one; the arrow is the work of turning it into a product with three sizes and a policy per size. The gap on the far left is the honest one: ordering a run and getting a vault back is not automated end to end, and the offline materials sandbox is not built. At our assumptions the margin is 39% to 50% a run, and the biggest cost under it is the person's time, not the tokens or the shared machine; automation is what widens it.

compute.reading: Here the heavy parts are someone else's commodity: EC2 by the hour, GPUs as a product. What we add is small and sits on the left: a launcher that makes one machine per task, and a vault born inside it so the keys never leave. The arrow is turning "a machine for your task" from a quote into a menu of three sizes. The price is a £20 platform fee plus twice the EC2 cost per 8-hour block, which pays for the person who starts the machine; the value is in the isolation the customer cannot easily build themselves. Not claimed: dedicated compute is not built, and SG Compute exists as sgraph tooling but is not connected to ruv.sgit runs; no run has been launched on it per order.

repo.reading: The repository already exists and is public in shape: a runner, specs, policies and a site, built on sgit and rUv's tools, run on the customer's own models and cloud. The subscription productises the upkeep: tested version bumps, the UI with their brand on it. What stays custom is the setup on each customer's infrastructure and the first policies written for them, which is where the expert offer joins. The margin is recurring and small per customer, and it rests on every layer under the runner being somebody's product or commodity; the risk is that the runner itself becomes a commodity, which is fine, because anybody who implements it implements sgit and ABPs.

expert.reading: The one offer that stays on the left. A person's judgement about what to run and what to allow is custom by nature, and the map says keep it there: it is the scarcest component and the highest margin. What we productise is the wrapper, fixed-price blocks instead of a day rate, and what we commoditise is the method, published so anyone can copy it. Every engagement leaves artefacts that sit further right, an ABP and a ledger of runs, which is how expert time pulls the other three offers along. Not automated, and not meant to be.
